title: Herb microgreen variety selection
subtitle: Choosing between basil, coriander, dill, and fennel as microgreen crops
excerpt: The four main herb microgreen crops (basil, coriander, dill, and fennel) each have distinct flavour profiles, different growing requirements, and different levels of growing difficulty. This guide compares them to help you decide which to grow first and which variety within each crop to use.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Penn State Extension indoor herb growing material. Herb microgreen growing comparisons synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The gel layer that forms around basil seeds when they are exposed to water. This property means basil must be sown dry and watered only from below — pre-soaking or top-watering causes the seeds to clump in an unmovable mass. It is the main practical difference between basil and other herb microgreen crops.

Buying seed specifically for microgreen growing requires checking that the seed is untreated (no fungicide or pesticide coating). This applies to all herb microgreen crops; seed sold in spice jars (dried dill seed, fennel seed, coriander seed) is often heat-treated and will not germinate reliably.

content.text: Herb microgreens give intense flavour from a small amount of cut cotyledon. Use them as a finishing element on food, not as a salad base. The four main herb crops each have a distinct flavour and a different growing requirement.
Growing difficulty: moderate. Basil needs the warmest conditions of any common herb microgreen (20 to 25°C), and has one critical rule: the seed must be sown dry.
makes the seed behave very differently from other herbs: sow dry, never pre-soak, and water only from below throughout the cycle. Beyond this, growing is straightforward.

Variety choice: Sweet basil (Genovese) is the standard and gives the classic sweet, anise-forward basil flavour. Purple basil varieties produce darker cotyledons with a slightly spicier taste. Lemon basil has a citrus note; cinnamon basil has a warm, spiced flavour.

Growing difficulty: moderate to challenging. Coriander takes 14 to 21 days and requires a hull-cracking step before sowing. The double-hulled seed slows germination if not cracked; even with preparation, germination rates are lower and less predictable than brassica or other herb microgreens.

Variety choice: all coriander varieties produce the same microgreens. Slow-bolting types are no different at the microgreen stage. Buy from a vegetable or microgreen seed supplier; spice coriander is often heat-treated and won't germinate.

Growing difficulty: easy. Dill microgreens are one of the simpler herb crops: no special seed preparation, reasonable germination rates, and a clear 10 to 14 day cycle. The feathery cotyledons have a concentrated dill flavour.

Variety choice: all dill varieties produce identical microgreens; the distinctions between Mammoth, Bouquet, Fernleaf, and other varieties only appear in mature plants. Buy untreated vegetable dill seed. Do not use dried dill seed from a spice jar; it is often heat-treated and will not germinate.

Growing difficulty: easy. Fennel microgreens follow the same method as dill: no special preparation, standard 10 to 14 day cycle, feathery fronds. The flavour is assertive anise; stronger than dill and useful in smaller quantities.

Variety choice: Florence fennel and common fennel both produce similar microgreens. The growth habit differences (Florence makes a large swollen base; common fennel does not) don't matter at the microgreen stage. Avoid fennel seed from the spice shelf; buy untreated vegetable seed instead.

: for dill, fennel, and coriander, buy from vegetable seed suppliers or microgreen seed suppliers rather than the spice aisle. Heat treatment of culinary seed is common and makes the seed non-viable for growing. Basil seed from garden suppliers is almost always untreated and suitable.
